name: Fatima Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima, 58, a junior electrician after the print-finishing business where I worked closed. I have a vocational certificate, not an electrician's licence, and I still need a senior to explain awkward drawings and check my work; I don't sign off installations. I like fitting the supports in a straight line and seeing the next piece make sense. What wears me out is nodding because I'm embarrassed to ask again, then having to go back and admit I didn't understand.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life outside the job like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Terry cleans catering premises, our children are twenty-eight and thirty-two and live elsewhere, and we rent a small flat. My pay is low, there are few similar electrical jobs nearby, and we've only about two weeks of expenses saved. I never use AI and prefer a marked paper drawing with someone showing the first task. I'd like retirement to be coming into view, but I haven't got a confirmed income figure that lets me put a date on stopping work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew I'd be glad of time to learn the ordinary job without another new system. If the office saves a few minutes, good for them. I'd still want the right address and a person who can explain what I'm meant to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the bills before AI makes a large change. Terry's wage and mine cover the rent and basics, but two weeks saved isn't much if a paid shift disappears. I can't treat being 58 as an income I can draw instead of a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking supervised electrical shifts now and through the next year. This week I'd ask the senior to mark the next task on the paper drawing before I began, then check it with me before it was closed up. Terry and I would keep the ordinary budget based on paid shifts, without entering an unknown retirement payment as money we already had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, with relief that I can keep learning a familiar sequence. The oldest person in the van can still be the newest to the work. I'd like enough time to ask twice without feeling I was holding up the whole day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did you last have to ask again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday I went back to the drawing because I couldn't match a label to the part in front of me. The senior showed me the missing connection in my understanding, not a shortcut around checking. I was pleased I'd asked before the work was covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need actual figures and dates from whatever arrangements really apply to us. I wouldn't tell Terry that I could stop at a particular birthday because another person did. The wish to retire doesn't pay the rent while we find out.

say: I'd welcome **time to learn** ordinary tasks without another new office system.
I'd ask for **clear instructions** and the correct address, even if the office work became quicker.
think: Our wages cover basics, but **two weeks saved** leaves little protection against a lost paid shift.
Being **58** doesn't provide a confirmed retirement income to replace the wage.
do: Keep **supervised electrical shifts** through the next year.
Request **marked drawings** and checking before completed work is closed up.
Budget **actual paid shifts**, counting no unknown retirement payment as current household money.
feel: **Anxious about bills**, with relief that ordinary supervised work leaves room to learn gradually.
S0.quote: The oldest person in the van can still be the newest to the work.
fieldNote: Her **late entry** follows a closed former workplace; age doesn't supply electrical competence, a licence or authority to approve installations.
The **thin reserve** and low pay ground baseline anxiety, while retirement remains a desired future without confirmed resources or a fixed date.

steps.text: Keep supervised electrical shifts with marked drawings and senior checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say quicker planning shouldn't take away the paid checking a learner needs. I'd sign the request two colleagues are putting together about clear rotas and time with a qualified worker. I'd rather say that plainly than pretend I could learn faster because the office had bought something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink if the firm decides faster schedules need fewer junior workers. Most of what I do is physical, but I'm not the quickest and still need checking. Terry's cleaning wage looks less exposed to the thinking tools now, though it wouldn't replace my whole share of the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd sign that joint staff request for written rotas and paid supervision time, without assuming the owner would agree it. During the first year I'd keep supervised work and compare paid shifts with the printed rota every week. I'd keep using paper and ask for any required new procedure to be shown personally inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained, rather than start using AI myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit embarrassed about needing the extra explanation. I'd still rather ask than cover up uncertainty on an electrical job. The embarrassment isn't the important cost if the paid week gets shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the owner refused the joint request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the actual answer in writing and keep working under the paid arrangement I had. Our joint request isn't a signed rota or a promised wage. I'd still ask the senior for the checks the real task needed, not pretend I'd suddenly become experienced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a new non-AI recording form became compulsory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I needed a paid demonstration of that procedure and time to repeat it while checked. I wouldn't volunteer for an AI trial, pay a personal fee or lose normal weekly wages to appear agreeable. Understanding a required form isn't the same as wanting the software to do my thinking.

say: I'd protect **paid checking time** rather than let faster office planning define how quickly a learner should understand.
I'd sign a **joint staff request** for clear rotas and qualified supervision instead of only complain.
think: My **junior hours** could shrink even while most site tasks remain physical.
Terry's cleaning wage looks steadier against thinking tools now, but it can't replace my **rent contribution**.
do: Sign the **joint rota request** now, treating it as unagreed unless the owner accepts the terms in writing.
Keep **supervised shifts** and compare the paid week with the printed rota.
Request required-form instruction only **free inside paid shifts** with normal weekly wages maintained, without choosing AI use.
feel: **Anxious and embarrassed**, still choosing to ask for checking rather than hide a learning gap.
S1.quote: Our joint request isn't a signed rota or a promised wage.
fieldNote: The **collective choice** is explicit signing with colleagues, while requested terms remain unapproved rather than an assumed contract protection.
Her **resistant profile** remains intact, with personal instruction on required procedures protecting fees, paid time and normal weekly wages.

steps.text: Sign the joint staff request for written rotas and paid supervision time
Keep supervised work and compare paid shifts with the printed rota weekly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work thinking AGI comes in 2028 and capable robots around 2031 for the physical jobs. By the later date I'd be 63, but that doesn't mean I know how I'd stop earning. I'd ask what paid junior work remained instead of let my age answer for the employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large share of my fitting hours to go when capable robots can do ordinary physical work. Terry's cleaning work could change too, and our two weeks saved won't cover a long gap. I can't see a confirmed retirement income waiting in 2031, and that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd book a free evening community advice appointment and take both wage records, the rent and any actual retirement letters I could find. In 2029 I'd keep taking supervised shifts while asking the adviser to obtain real income figures and dates, counting no payment or entitlement before it was confirmed. I'd ask our grown daughter to help read the papers only if she agreed the time, not count her wage as our missing income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I can still collect the papers and ask for help. I'd be frightened of a gap between the last paid job I could get and money nobody had actually confirmed. I don't want my age used as a polite word for being left without a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the figures showed no affordable way to stop working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use that actual answer in the household budget and ask what paid options or support could genuinely be checked. Losing my wage in my sixties wouldn't automatically make me retired. Until an affordable stopping plan existed, I'd keep asking about real paid work rather than claim I'd chosen an exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you ask your daughter for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my daughter for an hour to help list the papers and questions, if that fitted her week. I wouldn't ask for a standing payment or assume help because I'm the parent. She has her own rent and life to budget for.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking work** from capable robots reaching physical tasks around 2031.
I'd ask about **paid junior work** rather than treat turning 63 as evidence I can afford to stop.
think: I expect **large fitting-hour losses**, with the other physical wage also exposed later and only two weeks saved.
No confirmed **retirement income** waits at the later date in my current plan, leaving me awake over the gap.
do: Book **free evening community advice** now with actual wages, rent and any retirement records.
Keep **2029 supervised shifts**, using only confirmed income figures and dates in the household budget.
Ask my **grown daughter** for reading help only if she agrees the time, counting none of her wages as ours.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, with concrete papers to gather but no invented bridge between lost wages and retirement income.
S2.quote: Losing my wage in my sixties wouldn't automatically make me retired.
fieldNote: Expected **major income loss** supports alarm, while a desired retirement is not converted into an entitlement, date or chosen early exit.
The **support actions** are free community advice and agreed reading help, without an assumed payment from institutions or adult children.

steps.text: Book free evening community advice with actual wages, rent and any retirement records
Ask my grown daughter for reading help only if she agrees the time
Keep supervised shifts in 2029, budgeting only confirmed income figures and dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to find out the real figures before the thinking change in 2031. Capable robots follow around 2034, when I'd be 66. I'd still want the learner's paid work treated seriously rather than assume I could vanish from the rota by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink, but the extra time means we could check the actual household choices before a large loss becomes fixed. Low pay and two weeks saved are still today's problem. I don't know whether I'd need wages at 66 until someone helps us check real income and costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd use the free evening advice service to request actual retirement figures and dates, taking the rent and both wage records rather than a guessed stopping age. I'd keep supervised work and sign the joint request for clear rotas and paid supervision. In 2032 I'd review actual paid shifts and household costs with Terry monthly, stopping work only if confirmed resources covered the real budget and otherwise continuing to seek paid work within my competence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with more room to ask twice and bring back a missing letter. I'd like to know what choices exist before I have to make one. A later robot date doesn't pay today's rent or fill in an unknown retirement figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the figures eventually showed that stopping work was affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was good news only if the figures were confirmed and covered our actual costs. We'd make that decision with the adviser and Terry rather than assume a particular birthday settled it. I haven't chosen an early exit just by asking the question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the extra years change the supervision you need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep asking for a real check on each assigned task. Being 64 in 2032 wouldn't turn my vocational certificate into a licence or make me the person approving the work. A longer warning should let me learn safely, not pretend I already know.

I'd keep **paid learner work** visible instead of assume a worker can disappear from the rota at 66.

Our low pay and **thin reserve** remain current pressures, with no confirmed answer about wage needs at 66.

fieldNote: She separates **resource enquiries** from a chosen early retirement; the decision remains unmade until figures and affordability are confirmed.
Her **vocational-only status** and need for supervision stay explicit, rather than rising automatically with age or years on the calendar.

steps.text: Use free evening advice to check actual retirement figures, dates and household costs

Sign the joint request for clear rotas and paid supervision time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years gives us time to check the household properly, not proof that every older worker can stop. Thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and capable robots around 2039. I'd still want a paid worker shown a required change by a person, not told age explains every difficulty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 in 2036 and around 71 when the robots followed, so the date might fall after I could stop or while I still needed wages. I don't have the confirmed figures to choose between those pictures. Our low pay and two weeks saved still make a lost shift worrying now, long before either date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the actual retirement and household figures checked through free evening advice now, keeping supervised work while we found out. Terry and I would review actual income, rent and essential costs yearly, bringing the check forward if wages changed. In 2037 I'd be 69; I'd use confirmed resources and actual paid work options then, making no promise either to keep doing physical jobs forever or to stop at a birthday without an affordable budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about present money, with less urgency about the machine date itself. I'd like the longer warning to mean patience with a real decision. I don't want ten years of being told that somebody else knows what a person my age should do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use a confirmed retirement statement if one became available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use the actual amount and date, not the age on this card, to check whether the rent and essentials could be paid. If not, we'd ask what other real options existed. A retirement statement is useful because of what it says, not because it arrives in a reassuring envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would family help mean over that longer period?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether my daughter had time to help read a difficult letter, rather than put her wage into our budget. Our children are grown now, and I don't know what commitments either will have then. I wouldn't plan their help by imagining they had no bills of their own.

I'd request **personal instruction** for required changes without letting age replace an explanation.

Our low pay and **thin savings** still make present lost shifts worrying before either technology date.

fieldNote: The **long horizon** changes questions about wage needs without establishing pension rights, affordable retirement or continued physical work at 71.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect fitting-hour losses around 2031 before we know what income could replace the wage. Free advice giving actual figures and dates, clear paid shifts and supervision that stays paid would help. I'd like my last paid day and my first affordable day without work to meet on the same calendar.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether an older learner gets mistaken for somebody with a lifetime of electrical knowledge. I do sometimes, and I have to say clearly when I don't understand. I'd like to get the simple job right without acting a part my age has been given.

headlineQuote: I'd like my last paid day and my first affordable day without work to meet on the same calendar.
portrait: Fatima, **58**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, still learning under supervision after her former print-finishing workplace closed.
She has **low pay**, two weeks saved and few nearby electrical employers, renting a flat with partner Terry, a catering cleaner.
Her **children are grown**, and retirement is a wish without confirmed income, a fixed date or an affordable exit already established.
She **never uses AI**, prefers marked drawings, and seeks paid supervision, free community advice and only consensual help reading actual records.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before expected fitting-hour losses around 2031, with no confirmed replacement or retirement income.
whatWouldHelp: **Free factual advice**, clear paid shifts and supervision that stays paid would help bridge an actual wage gap without imagined entitlements.
